title: How Cerebral Palsy Works
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss cerebral palsy: an umbrella term for conditions caused by brain injury affecting movement, not a disease. They cover prevalence (about 8,000 US children a year, more common in boys and premature births), history from Dr. John Little (1853) through Sir William Osler's coining of the term, Freud's ideas, and the Goldensons' United Cerebral Palsy association and Marie Killilea's books. Causes are grouped by timing: pregnancy (infections like toxoplasmosis and rubella, preeclampsia, jaundice from blood type incompatibility), birth injuries (about 5-10%, such as breech, prolapsed cord, asphyxia), and after-birth injuries up to age 2-3 (drowning, choking, meningitis). Types are spastic (hemiplegia, diplegia, quadriplegia), athetoid/dyskinetic, and ataxic. Diagnosis, therapies, medications (baclofen pump, Botox), surgery, experimental stem cell therapy, and a head transplant news item are discussed. Closing segments cover famous people with CP, listener mail about ice density and the meaning of "factoid", and sign-off.

segments.title: What cerebral palsy is and prevalence
segments.summary: CP is an umbrella term for conditions caused by brain injury affecting movement, not a disease. Stats: about 8,000 children born with it each year; most common childhood physical disability; more common in boys and premature births.

segments.title: History: John Little, Osler, Freud, and early advocates
segments.summary: Dr. John Little's 1853 work on birth injuries and his narrow theory; William Osler coined the term cerebral palsy; Freud's theory of prenatal causes; Leonard and Isabel Goldenson founded the United Cerebral Palsy Association; Marie Killilea's books Karen and With Love from Karen raised public awareness.

segments.title: Causes: birth injuries and prenatal factors
segments.summary: Birth injuries account for roughly 5-10% of cases, including breech delivery, prolonged labor, forceps, prolapsed or wrapped umbilical cord. Prenatal causes include infections such as toxoplasmosis and rubella, maternal diabetes and epilepsy, preeclampsia reducing blood flow, and jaundice from blood type incompatibility.

segments.title: Postnatal causes and the brain development window
segments.summary: Cerebral palsy can result from injuries after birth up to about age two or three, such as drowning, choking, or meningitis, since the brain is developed by then. Shaken baby syndrome is mentioned as a controversial topic for a future episode.

segments.title: Prevention: magnesium sulfate and therapeutic hypothermia
segments.summary: A 2008 New England Journal of Medicine study found magnesium sulfate given to high-risk preterm mothers roughly halved CP rates; therapeutic hypothermia lowers metabolism to reduce brain damage from oxygen deprivation.

segments.title: Types of cerebral palsy: spastic, athetoid, ataxic
segments.summary: CP is classified by symptoms into spastic (the largest group, with quadriplegia, hemiplegia, diplegia subtypes), athetoid/dyskinetic (involuntary slow movements, shifting tone), and ataxic (balance and fine motor problems, intention tremor). Spasticity is explained as muscle tone controlled by a brain-spinal cord-muscle interplay; damage to the brain's relaxation signal leads to rigid muscles and deformity over time.

segments.title: Diagnosis, therapy, and early intervention
segments.summary: Signs in infants include weak or tight muscles, dragging legs when crawling, scissoring, toe walking, and poor balance. Treatment focuses on managing symptoms through massage, muscle development, speech, occupational therapy, and communication methods; early intervention helps because the brain is plastic. Christy Brown is mentioned as an example of using his left foot to make art, and the 'My Left Foot' film with Daniel Day-Lewis is discussed.

segments.title: Medications, surgery, stem cells, and head transplant tangent
segments.summary: Muscle relaxers like diazepam and Botox reduce spasticity; baclofen delivered by an implanted pump can be used but risks overdose. Surgeries untwist bones and selective dorsal rhizotomy cuts nerve fibers as a last resort. Stem cell therapies are in clinical trials, and some companies sell unproven treatments. The hosts then discuss an Italian surgeon's planned head transplant.

segments.title: Outlook, intellectual disability, and famous people with CP
segments.summary: Life expectancy is normal, though mobility can worsen. Intellectual disability can co-occur but is not inherent; people with speech difficulties are often wrongly assumed to have intellectual disabilities. Famous people mentioned include Jerry Jewel, Josh Blue, RJ Mitte, Abby Nicole Curran, Jerry Trailer, Stephen Hopkins, and a blog about a girl named Maya.

segments.title: Listener mail: ice density and factoid
segments.summary: A listener's question about good news versus bad news first, and a correction about the Icebergs episode regarding ice density; the hosts also explain that factoid originally meant a false fact accepted as true, coined by Norman Mailer, and now often means a trivial fact.
